title: mathviz example
Theming
text:
Everything mathviz draws – panel chrome, slider tracks, the legend, chart axes and gridlines, the chart palette – is a CSS custom property with a --vm- prefix. The CSS reads them the ordinary way; the JavaScript reads them with getComputedStyle at call time, so a chart built after a theme toggle sees the new values. To re-theme the library you redeclare tokens. There is no JavaScript configuration for colors.
VM = window.VM
vmTheme = Generators.observe(notify => VM.plotting.onThemeChange(notify))
chartColors = VM.plotting.colors(vmTheme)

title: Theming
Theming
text:
The tokens
Live: each swatch is the value your browser computes for the token right now. Toggle the theme and watch the column change.

{
  vmTheme
  const rows = [
    ["Chrome", null],
    ["--vm-bg", "page background: fullscreen backdrop, the pill behind the fullscreen button, slider thumb ring, swatch tint base"],
    ["--vm-surface", "panel and controls-bar background; tooltip background (JS)"],
    ["--vm-surface-hover", "hover state of modebar and fullscreen buttons"],
    ["--vm-text", "panel text; chart font and tooltip text (JS)"],
    ["--vm-text-soft", "labels, the legend's unchecked items, play buttons; axis ticks and titles, the empty-state message (JS)"],
    ["--vm-border", "panel borders, slider tracks; axis lines, zero lines, ticks, tooltip border (JS)"],
    ["--vm-accent", "buttons, focus rings, slider fill, the active modebar button"],
    ["--vm-accent-hover", "Observable Inputs button hover"],
    ["--vm-grid", "chart gridlines (JS only)"],
    ["--vm-radius", "panel and popover corners -- same in both themes"],
    ["--vm-radius-sm", "inputs, buttons, the legend grip -- same in both themes"],
    ["--vm-shadow", "legend, popover, modebar pill"],
    ["--vm-font-sans", "chart text and the playback popover -- same in both themes. Redeclare it if your site self-hosts a font"],
    ["Chart palette (VM.plotting.colors())", null],
    ["--vm-color-fn", "the function itself, the primary trace"],
    ["--vm-color-alt", "an alternate or reference trace; .vm-swatch-alt; .vm-invalid"],
    ["--vm-color-ok", "a converged or correct marker; .vm-swatch-ok"],
    ["--vm-color-muted", "de-emphasized data"],
    ["--vm-color-ink", "strokes and labels that should read as text"],
    ["--vm-color-warn", "a warning, a diverging iterate; .vm-swatch-warn"],
    ["--vm-color-accent2", "a third series; .vm-swatch-accent2"],
    ["--vm-color-accent3", "a fourth series"],
    ["--vm-color-halo", "the ring around a marker: white on light, the page background on dark"]
  ]
  const style = getComputedStyle(document.body)
  const table = document.createElement("table")
  table.className = "table table-sm small"
  table.innerHTML = "<thead><tr><th>Token</th><th>Current value</th><th>Used for</th></tr></thead>"
  const body = document.createElement("tbody")
  for (const [name, use] of rows) {
    const tr = document.createElement("tr")
    if (use === null) { tr.innerHTML = `<th colspan=3 style="padding-top:.8rem">${name}</th>`; body.appendChild(tr); continue }
    const value = style.getPropertyValue(name).trim()
    const isColor = /^(#|rgb)/.test(value)
    const chip = isColor ? `<span style="display:inline-block;width:1rem;height:1rem;border-radius:3px;border:1px solid var(--vm-border);background:${value};vertical-align:-3px;margin-right:.4rem"></span>` : ""
    tr.innerHTML = `<td style="white-space:nowrap"><code>${name}</code></td><td style="white-space:nowrap">${chip}<code>${value}</code></td><td>${use}</td>`
    body.appendChild(tr)
  }
  table.appendChild(body)
  return table
}






The palette is keyed by role, not hue. A page reads chartColors.fn and chartColors.alt rather than repeating a hex, so redefining --vm-color-fn recolors every primary trace on the site. halo deserves a word: pages used to write line: {color: "white"} for the ring around a marker, which is a white ring on a near-black chart in dark mode. Use chartColors.halo.
Only these tokens are public. The library also writes a few custom properties at runtime for its own layout – --sx (a slider’s fill fraction), --vm-plot-aspect-ratio, --vm-fs-plot-width, --vm-svg-aspect (fullscreen letterboxing) and --vm-swatch (a swatch’s tint). Treat them as reserved; don’t set them.

title: Theming
text:
Dark mode
The library decides “dark” by testing one selector list against <body> and then <html>:
body.quarto-dark, html[data-bs-theme="dark"], body[data-bs-theme="dark"], html.vm-dark, body.vm-dark

body.quarto-dark – what Quarto’s built-in light/dark toggle sets
[data-bs-theme="dark"] on html or body – Bootstrap 5.3’s convention
.vm-dark on html or body – for a site with its own toggle: add the class and the library follows

The same list appears in two places – the dark block in tokens.css, and settings.darkSelector in chart-theme.js – and they must stay identical. If your toggle uses none of these, either add .vm-dark to <html> when it flips, or name your own selector:
VM.plotting.configure({darkSelector: "html.theme-dark"})
and declare your dark tokens under that same selector.






Keep the selector root-scoped



A bare [data-bs-theme="dark"] looks equivalent but isn’t: Quarto sets that attribute directly on its <nav> to force a dark navbar on an otherwise-light page, and custom properties inherit down the DOM – so an unscoped match painted the entire dark palette into the navbar. Match on html or body only.



Why JS reads from <body>
The light tokens are declared on :root, but the dark ones under selectors that match <body> (Quarto flips a body class). So getComputedStyle(document.documentElement) returns the light value even in dark mode – <html> never matches the dark block. Every --vm-* read in the library goes through document.body for this reason. If you write your own token-reading code, do the same; this exact mistake once turned every chart tooltip into a white box on the dark theme.


Two-step toggles
Quarto’s toggle flips the body class and swaps the stylesheet as separate steps, class first. A callback that reads tokens synchronously on the class change sees the outgoing theme’s values. onThemeChange waits two animation frames before notifying for exactly this reason, and compares the theme name inside that wait so unrelated body-class changes (a sidebar opening) don’t fire it. Use it rather than your own MutationObserver.

title: Theming
text:
Prose swatches
To tint a color word in running text so it matches the trace it describes: <span class="vm-swatch vm-swatch-alt">red</span> → red. Five modifiers exist – -alt, -ok, -warn, -accent2 map to the matching palette token, -accent to --vm-accent. vm-swatch alone sets no color. There is no -fn, -muted, -ink, -accent3 or -halo swatch.

title: Theming
text:
Bringing your own stylesheet
mathviz: {css: false} (or simply not loading mathviz.css) leaves you responsible for both halves: the --vm-* tokens the JS reads (it falls back to the light defaults without them – fine on a light-only site, wrong in dark mode) and the ojs-* / vm-* rules that lay out panels and position the legend. Most sites want the stylesheet plus a handful of token overrides, not a replacement.

title: VM.sampling
text:
Two generator factories. Each returns a zero-argument function you call for the next value, so a page seeds once and draws as many samples as it needs – and because the seed can live in the URL, a link reproduces exactly the same “random” data.

VM = window.VM







VM.sampling.seededRandom(seed)
A deterministic mulberry32 generator: the same seed always produces the same sequence.








Parameter
Type
Description




seed
number
Coerced to a 32-bit unsigned integer (seed >>> 0), so 1.7 and 1 are the same seed.



Returns () => number, uniform on [0, 1).

viewof seed = Inputs.range([0, 9999], {label: "seed", step: 1, value: 42})







{
  const rng = VM.sampling.seededRandom(seed)
  const out = []
  for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) out.push(rng().toFixed(4))
  return out
}








VM.sampling.gaussianRandom(rng)
Box-Muller transform: turns a uniform generator into a standard-normal one (mean 0, variance 1). For any other normal, scale and shift the output: mean + sd * gaussian().








Parameter
Type
Description




rng
() => number
A uniform [0, 1) generator – typically seededRandom’s return value. Two draws are consumed per sample.



Returns () => number, standard normal.

{
  const gaussian = VM.sampling.gaussianRandom(VM.sampling.seededRandom(seed))
  let sum = 0, sumSq = 0
  const n = 10000
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { const z = gaussian(); sum += z; sumSq += z * z }
  const mean = sum / n
  return html`Over ${n} draws: mean <b>${mean.toFixed(3)}</b>, variance <b>${(sumSq / n - mean * mean).toFixed(3)}</b>`
}






See the distribution explorer recipe for these feeding a histogram under a theoretical curve.

title: VM.numerical
text:
Pure functions over plain arrays and {x, y} points. None of them validate their inputs beyond what is noted; they are written to be read by a mathematics audience, so each is the textbook algorithm with no surprises inside.
VM = window.VM

title: VM.numerical
text:
Fitting

VM.numerical.linearRegression(points)
Ordinary least-squares fit of a line y = slope·x + intercept. Every convergence-order plot uses this on (log h, log error) pairs – the slope is the observed order.








Parameter
Type
Description




points
{x, y}[]
The data, in the order the fitted segment should be drawn.



Returns {slope, intercept, xlo, xhi} | null – null if there are fewer than two points or the x-values don’t vary (a vertical, degenerate fit).






Note



xlo and xhi are the first and last point’s x, not the min and max. They exist for drawing the fitted segment across the data, which is only what they describe when points is sorted by x.



{
  const pts = []
  for (let i = 1; i <= 6; i++) pts.push({x: i, y: 2 * i + 1 + (i % 2 === 0 ? 0.1 : -0.1)})
  return VM.numerical.linearRegression(pts)
}








VM.numerical.l1Regression(points, opts?)
Least-absolute-deviations (L1) line fit, via iteratively reweighted least squares seeded from linearRegression. Far less sensitive to a few large outliers than L2: an outlier’s residual is down-weighted in proportion to its own size instead of being squared.









Parameter
Type
Default
Description




points
{x, y}[]

The data, in drawing order.


opts.maxIterations
number
100
Cap on reweighting passes.


opts.tolerance
number
1e-10
Stop once |Δslope| + |Δintercept| falls below this.


opts.epsilon
number
1e-6
Floor on |residual| in the weight 1 / max(|residual|, epsilon), so a point the line passes through exactly doesn’t get infinite weight.



Returns {slope, intercept, xlo, xhi, iterations} | null – the fit plus the number of passes taken; null under the same conditions as linearRegression.

{
  // Five points on y = x, plus one wild outlier. L2 is dragged toward it; L1 is not.
  const pts = [{x: 1, y: 1}, {x: 2, y: 2}, {x: 3, y: 3}, {x: 4, y: 4}, {x: 5, y: 5}, {x: 6, y: 30}]
  return {l2: VM.numerical.linearRegression(pts), l1: VM.numerical.l1Regression(pts)}
}








VM.numerical.polynomialFit(mathjs, points, degree)
Least-squares polynomial fit of a given degree, solved from the normal equations with math.js’s LU solver (plain Gaussian elimination loses too much precision once degree approaches the point count).



Parameter
Type
Description




mathjs
math.js instance
Does the linear algebra.


points
{x, y}[]
At least degree + 1 of them.


degree
number
Degree of the polynomial.



Returns {coeffs, evaluate, totalSquaredError} | null:

coeffs – [c0, c1, …, c_degree], in increasing power
evaluate – the fitted polynomial as (x) => number
totalSquaredError – the sum of squared residuals over points

null if there are fewer points than coefficients or the system is singular.

{
  const pts = []
  for (let x = -2; x <= 2; x++) pts.push({x, y: x * x - 1})
  const fit = VM.numerical.polynomialFit(math, pts, 2)
  return {coeffs: fit.coeffs, at3: fit.evaluate(3), error: fit.totalSquaredError}
}

title: VM.numerical
text:
ODE steppers
Both take the same arguments and return the same shape, so a page switches methods by swapping the function.

VM.numerical.eulerSolve(f, t0, y0, tEnd, n)
Forward Euler for y' = f(t, y), y(t0) = y0, with n fixed steps of h = (tEnd − t0) / n.



Parameter
Type
Description




f
(t, y) => number
The right-hand side – see makeFunction2.


t0, y0
number
Initial condition.


tEnd
number
Final time.


n
number
Number of steps. Not validated: n = 0 gives an infinite step and a single-point trajectory.



Returns {ts: number[], ys: number[]} – n + 1 samples each, starting at (t0, y0).


VM.numerical.rk4Solve(f, t0, y0, tEnd, n)
The classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method. Same parameters and return shape as eulerSolve.

viewof odeSteps = Inputs.range([2, 64], {label: "steps n", step: 1, value: 8})







{
  // y' = y, y(0) = 1, so y(1) = e. Watch the two errors shrink as n grows.
  const f = (t, y) => y
  const euler = VM.numerical.eulerSolve(f, 0, 1, 1, odeSteps)
  const rk4 = VM.numerical.rk4Solve(f, 0, 1, 1, odeSteps)
  const last = arr => arr[arr.length - 1]
  return html`Euler error: <b>${Math.abs(last(euler.ys) - Math.E).toExponential(2)}</b>   RK4 error: <b>${Math.abs(last(rk4.ys) - Math.E).toExponential(2)}</b>`
}

title: VM.numerical
text:
Quadrature and interpolation

VM.numerical.simpsonEstimate(f, lo, hi, n)
Composite Simpson’s rule on n subintervals.








Parameter
Type
Description




f
(x) => number
The integrand.


lo, hi
number
The limits.


n
number
Number of subintervals. Must be even. This is not validated; an odd n silently applies the wrong weights.



Returns number.






Warning



Samples where f is not finite – a pole, a domain error – are skipped (they contribute zero), including the endpoints. So simpsonEstimate(x => 1/x, 0, 1, n) returns a finite, wrong number rather than Infinity. This is deliberate for a page where a reader is typing the integrand: one bad point shouldn’t blank the whole estimate. Check the integrand yourself if you need a hard failure.



VM.numerical.simpsonEstimate(Math.sin, 0, Math.PI, 10)   // exact value 2








VM.numerical.lagrangeQuadratic(x0, y0, x1, y1, x2, y2, sampleCount)
Samples the unique quadratic through three points – the parabola one Simpson panel integrates – at sampleCount + 1 evenly spaced abscissae from x0 to x2 inclusive, so it can be drawn.








Parameter
Type
Description




x0, y0, x1, y1, x2, y2
number
The three points. The x-values must be distinct; a repeat divides by zero and fills ys with Infinity/NaN.


sampleCount
number
Number of intervals between samples.



Returns {xs: number[], ys: number[]} with sampleCount + 1 points.

VM.numerical.lagrangeQuadratic(0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 4, 4)   // the parabola y = x² sampled at 0, .5, 1, 1.5, 2

title: VM.distributions
text:
Helpers

VM.distributions.logGamma(x)
ln Γ(x) by Lanczos approximation (g = 7, n = 9; reflection formula below 0.5), accurate to ~15 significant digits for x > 0. The shared building block behind every normalizing constant here; useful directly for log(n choose k) = logGamma(n+1) − logGamma(k+1) − logGamma(n−k+1).








Parameter
Type
Description




x
number
Any real except 0 and the negative integers (poles); those return Infinity/NaN with no guard.



Returns number.

[VM.distributions.logGamma(5), Math.log(24), VM.distributions.logGamma(0.5), Math.log(Math.sqrt(Math.PI))]








VM.distributions.sampleCurve(fn, lo, hi, opts?)
Samples a function over [lo, hi] into parallel arrays ready for a Plotly trace or a Plot.line.









Parameter
Type
Default
Description




fn
(x) => number

Typically a *Pdf/*Pmf with its parameters bound: x => VM.distributions.normalPdf(x, 0, 1).


lo, hi
number

The range, both ends inclusive.


opts.discrete
boolean
false
Evaluate only at the integers from ceil(lo) to floor(hi) – what a PMF has support on – instead of on a fine grid. opts.n is ignored; the arrays are empty if no integer lies in the range.


opts.n
number
400
Number of evenly spaced samples in continuous mode. n = 1 divides by zero.



Returns {xs: number[], ys: number[]}.

VM.distributions.sampleCurve(k => VM.distributions.poissonPmf(k, 2), 0, 5, {discrete: true})








VM.distributions.histogramBins(samples, binCount, range?)
Bins an array of draws into equal-width bins, normalized to densities so the bars’ total area is ~1 and a theoretical curve overlays directly.









Parameter
Type
Default
Description




samples
number[]

The draws.


binCount
number

Number of bins (≥ 1).


range
{lo, hi}
samples’ min/max
A fixed bin range. Pass {lo: min − 0.5, hi: max + 0.5} with binCount = max − min + 1 for one bin centered on each integer. Samples outside an explicit range are clamped into the first/last bin, not dropped. A zero-width range is widened to [lo − 0.5, hi + 0.5].



Returns {edges: number[], centers: number[], densities: number[]} – binCount + 1 edges; binCount centers and densities, where densities[i] = count[i] / (samples.length · width). All three arrays are empty when samples is empty or binCount < 1.

{
  const gaussian = VM.sampling.gaussianRandom(VM.sampling.seededRandom(1))
  const draws = []
  for (let i = 0; i < 2000; i++) draws.push(gaussian())
  return VM.distributions.histogramBins(draws, 6, {lo: -3, hi: 3})
}






See the distribution explorer recipe for the histogram-under-a-curve chart.

title: VM.distributions
text:
Discrete masses
All return 0 when k is not an integer in the support.

VM.distributions.bernoulliPmf(k, p)
P(K = 1) = p, P(K = 0) = 1 − p; 0 for any other k. p is not validated.


VM.distributions.binomialPmf(k, n, p)
Exactly k successes in n independent trials with success probability p. p ≤ 0 puts all mass on k = 0, p ≥ 1 all mass on k = n.


VM.distributions.poissonPmf(k, lambda)
λ^k e^{−λ} / k! for integer k ≥ 0. lambda ≤ 0 puts all mass on k = 0.


VM.distributions.geometricPmf(k, p)
Trials until the first success: (1 − p)^{k−1} p for k = 1, 2, 3, … – not the competing “failures before the first success” convention whose support starts at 0. p is not validated.


VM.distributions.negativeBinomialPmf(k, r, p)
Trials until the r-th success, so the support is k = r, r+1, … and r = 1 is exactly geometricPmf. 0 when p is outside (0, 1]; p = 1 puts all mass on k = r.


VM.distributions.hypergeometricPmf(k, N, K, n)
Exactly k successes when drawing n items without replacement from a population of N containing K successes: C(K, k)·C(N−K, n−k) / C(N, n). Support is max(0, n − (N − K)) ≤ k ≤ min(n, K); 0 there and for any invalid (N, K, n).

title: VM.distributions
text:
Continuous densities

VM.distributions.exponentialPdf(x, rate)
Mean 1 / rate. 0 for x < 0 or rate ≤ 0.


VM.distributions.normalPdf(x, mean, variance)
Parameterized by variance, not standard deviation: pass sd * sd. 0 for variance ≤ 0.


VM.distributions.gammaPdf(x, shape, rate)
Parameterized by rate, not scale: the mean is shape / rate. For a scale θ pass 1 / θ. Valid for any real shape > 0. 0 for x ≤ 0 or a non-positive parameter.


VM.distributions.chiSquaredPdf(x, k)
k degrees of freedom – exactly gammaPdf(x, k/2, 1/2).


VM.distributions.betaPdf(x, a, b)
On the open interval (0, 1): 0 at and outside the endpoints, so betaPdf(0, 1, 1) is 0 even though the density is 1 on the interior. 0 for a non-positive shape.


VM.distributions.studentTPdf(x, k)
k degrees of freedom, any real k > 0 (not only an integer). 0 for k ≤ 0.


VM.distributions.fPdf(x, d1, d2)
d1 numerator and d2 denominator degrees of freedom. 0 for x ≤ 0 or a non-positive parameter.


VM.distributions.lognormalPdf(x, mean, variance)
The density of e^X for X ~ Normal(mean, variance). The parameters describe the underlying normal, not the log-normal’s own mean (exp(μ + σ²/2)) and variance. 0 for x ≤ 0 or variance ≤ 0.


VM.distributions.cauchyPdf(x, location, scale)
The Cauchy has no mean and no variance, so location is its median and scale its half-width at half-maximum. 0 for scale ≤ 0.


VM.distributions.weibullPdf(x, shape, scale)
Parameterized by scale, not rate, so shape = 1 is the exponential with rate 1 / scale. Shape below 1 gives a failure rate that falls with age, above 1 one that rises. 0 for x < 0 or a non-positive parameter; at x = 0 the density is 1/scale when shape = 1 and 0 otherwise.

How it’s put together
text: A short map of the repository and the handful of decisions that shape it. The working rules for contributors – headers, style, the release checklist – are in CONTRIBUTING.md; the deeper “why” behind each invariant, written as instructions for someone editing the code, is in CLAUDE.md.

title: How it’s put together
text:
Layout
_extensions/mathviz/   the Quarto extension: _extension.yml, mathviz.lua, dist/ (copied by the build)
dist/                  the generated bundle, committed (jsDelivr serves it by tag); never hand-edited
src/manifest.mjs       THE load order, for the build and the tests
src/js/<category>/     one VM.<category>.<name> per file; tests colocated as <name>.test.js
src/css/               tokens.css first, then one file per concern
scripts/               build.mjs (concatenate + syntax-check), load-vm.mjs (test loader)
docs/                  this site; example.qmd at the root is the CI smoke render

title: How it’s put together
How it’s put together
text:
The build is a concatenation
scripts/build.mjs reads the manifest, joins the files with a separator, syntax-checks the result with node --check, writes dist/mathviz.{js,css} and copies both into _extensions/mathviz/dist/. No bundler, no minifier, no dependencies: the output is the readable source with // ---- src/js/… ---- markers, so a stack trace in a consumer’s browser points at a recognizable file, and the JSDoc travels with it.
The one subtlety is the separator. For JS it is a lone ;. Each file ends in a call – })(window), or })() for a module with nothing to export – and two of those back to back parse as })(window)(function …): the first file’s return value called with the second file as its argument. That is syntactically valid, so node --check can’t catch it, and the page dies after the first file with (intermediate value)(...) is not a function. The semicolon makes each file its own statement.
dist/ is committed because both distribution channels serve the repository as-is: quarto add downloads an archive and runs nothing, and jsDelivr serves files straight from a tag. CI rebuilds and fails on a diff, so src/ and dist/ can’t drift.

title: How it’s put together
text:
Tests run the real files
scripts/load-vm.mjs evaluates every manifest entry, in order, into the Node process’s global scope (indirect eval, so the IIFEs see a window), with a minimal document and Plotly stub for the modules that touch them at load time. The *.test.js files import it and test VM.* – the production code, not re-implementations. node --test finds them; math.js is the only dev dependency, for the expression tests.
Two tests guard the documentation itself: manifest.test.js (above) and docs-coverage.test.js, which fails if any VM.* member lacks a ### VM.<category>.<name> heading in docs/reference/, or a heading names something that doesn’t exist.

title: How it’s put together
section: The version is in three places
text:
The version is in three places
package.json, _extensions/mathviz/_extension.yml and VERSION in mathviz.lua. The build refuses to run unless they agree. The Lua one names the site_libs/quarto-contrib/mathviz-<version>/ folder in a consumer’s output, which is what busts their browser cache on upgrade.

title: How it’s put together
text:
The Lua filter’s odd shape
mathviz.lua adds one HTML dependency per vendor <script> tag (mathviz-mathjs, mathviz-plotly, mathviz-referrer), each before the mathviz dependency that carries the bundle. Three facts about Quarto’s dependency handling, verified against Quarto 1.7’s source, force this:

quarto.doc.include_text("in-header", …) lands in header-includes, which is emitted below the whole dependency block – so a Plotly tag added that way loads after mathviz.js, and the patch finds no Plotly to patch.
Within one dependency, scripts entries are emitted before the head string, so the vendor tags can’t share the bundle’s dependency.
Quarto’s injectHtml iterates a live children collection while moving nodes out of it, so a head string holding several tags loses every second one. One tag per dependency is the workaround.

scripts/stylesheets entries must be local files (Quarto copies them into site_libs), hence raw <script> tags in head for the CDN URLs. A head-only dependency creates no site_libs folder.

title: How it’s put together
text:
Theme detection
Two places hold the dark-mode selector list and must stay identical: the :where(…) block in src/css/tokens.css, and settings.darkSelector in src/js/plotting/chart-theme.js. The CSS half declares the dark tokens; the JS half decides themeName(). The Theming page covers the consequences: why the tokens are read from <body>, why onThemeChange waits two frames and compares before firing, why the selectors are root-scoped.

title: How it’s put together
text:
Self-installing modules
Slider playback, the draggable legend, the SVG fullscreen button and the slider-track fill share a pattern: a MutationObserver on document.body plus delegated document-level listeners, so they enhance elements Observable Inputs creates at runtime and recreates on every upstream change – there is no single moment at which “all the sliders exist” to wire them up individually. Each marks what it has enhanced (data-vm-play-ready, data-vm-draggable) to stay idempotent. plotly-fullscreen-button.js does the same job for Plotly by wrapping Plotly.newPlot/react, since there is no DOM to watch before the chart exists.

title: How it’s put together
text:
Style
Explicit for/while loops and if/else over .map()/.filter()/.reduce() chains and ternaries, throughout src/js. The code is read by a mathematics audience more at home in Python than in functional JavaScript. Callbacks an API requires (Plotly config values, Plot accessors, addEventListener) are the exception.

title: Your first chart
Your first chart
text:
Cell by cell

The panel
::: {.ojs-panel .ojs-row}
```{ojs}
viewof fText = Inputs.text({label: "f(x)", value: "sin(x) + x/3"})
```
```{ojs}
viewof k = Inputs.range([1, 5], {label: "Frequency", step: 0.1, value: 1})
```
:::
A Quarto div with two classes. ojs-panel is the chrome – border, background, radius, and restyling of every input inside it. ojs-row is the layout: a flex row that wraps, with the first control stretching to fill. Both are plain CSS from the bundle; the full list of classes is in the markup contract.
The slider gets its play button for free – the playback module finds every range slider inside a panel.


The theme pair
vmTheme = Generators.observe(notify => VM.plotting.onThemeChange(notify))
chartColors = VM.plotting.colors(vmTheme)
The two most important lines on any chart page, and the ones most often left out.
onThemeChange calls notify("light") (or "dark") now and after every toggle, and returns a teardown – exactly the shape Generators.observe wants – so vmTheme is a reactive cell that changes value when the theme does. colors() ignores its argument; colors(vmTheme) is written that way so chartColors depends on vmTheme and re-runs too. And then so does mainPlot, because it reads chartColors.fn.
Why this is necessary: the chart’s chrome – background, axes, gridlines, tooltip – is re-themed for you (the Plotly patch runs a relayout on every chart when the theme flips). But chartColors.fn is a value the page baked into a trace. Nothing but re-running the cell can change it. Without these two lines the axes go dark and the line stays light-mode blue.


The function
const f = VM.expressions.makeFunction(math, fText)
math is the math.js global the extension loaded. makeFunction returns a (x) => number, or null if the text won’t parse; it never throws. The returned function gives NaN where evaluation fails (sqrt(x) at x = -1), which Plotly draws as a gap.


The sampling loop
for (let i = 0; i <= 400; i++) {
  const x = -6 + 12 * i / 400
  xs.push(x)
  ys.push(f ? f(k * x) : NaN)
}
An explicit loop, on purpose. The library is written for readers more at home in Python than in functional JavaScript, and the pages that use it follow suit. (VM.distributions.sampleCurve does this loop for you when the function is a density.)


The chart
const div = document.createElement("div")
div.className = "plotly-box-large"
Plotly.newPlot(div, [...], VM.plotting.layout({...}), VM.plotting.config())
VM.plotting.autoResize(div)
return div
The standard OJS idiom: build a detached div, draw into it, return it and let Observable put it on the page. Three library calls:

VM.plotting.layout({...}) – the themed layout, with the page’s own xaxis/yaxis/annotations deep-merged on top. On a page rendered through the extension this is technically redundant (the patch merges it under every newPlot), but writing it makes the dependency visible and works on a page without the patch.
VM.plotting.config() – {responsive: true, displaylogo: false}.
VM.plotting.autoResize(div) – the chart is built detached, so Plotly measured 0×0. This resizes it once it lands, and stops when the div is replaced by a re-run (a bare ResizeObserver would outlive it and throw).

plotly-box-large is the one size class the CSS ships: full width, 72vh tall with a 500px floor. Set your own height for anything else.


The empty state
annotations: f ? [] : VM.plotting.emptyState("Couldn't parse that expression")
When f is null every y is NaN and Plotly draws an empty grid – which looks identical to a valid function that happens to be off-screen. emptyState puts a message in the middle so the reader knows it’s their input.


The chart block
::: {.ojs-chart-block}
...
:::
The wrapper around the chart cells. It is the positioning anchor for a floating legend, and it is what the fullscreen button fullscreens – so a legend or a controls bar inside it comes along. Every chart wants one, even a chart with neither, so that adding them later is a matter of dropping in a cell.

text:
mathviz is the machinery behind Visual Math Lab, packaged so any site can use it: a Quarto extension that drops into an OJS page with one line of front matter, and the same code as a plain script bundle for everything else.
Every chart, panel and slider on this site is drawn by the library itself. Toggle the theme in the navbar and watch them follow.

title: mathviz
text:
What you get

Themed charts. Plotly and Observable Plot read the same fonts, grid, palette and tooltip style from CSS custom properties, live – so charts follow your site’s light/dark toggle and re-theme the instant it flips. The Plotly patch does this to every chart on the page with no per-page code.
A modebar worth using. Fullscreen, gentler zoom steps, pan by default, no box/lasso select.
Control-panel CSS that lays Observable Inputs.* out into a tidy panel, and keeps step sliders directly above a chart – also in fullscreen.
Slider playback: every range slider in a panel gets a play/pause button with speed and loop/bounce options.
A floating, draggable legend that toggles traces and remembers where you put it.
Numerical helpers: safe expression parsing via math.js, ODE steppers, quadrature, least-squares, sixteen closed-form densities, seeded random numbers, 1-D filters, Sperner triangulations.

title: Installing
text: mathviz ships two ways from one source tree. Both give you the same window.VM, the same CSS, and the same self-installing behaviour.

title: Installing
text:
Quarto site, book or document
quarto add apurvanakade/mathviz
This copies the extension into _extensions/apurvanakade/mathviz/ in your project. Enable it project-wide in _quarto.yml, or per page in front matter:
filters:
  - mathviz
The filter adds four things to every HTML page’s <head>, in this order:

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjs@15.2.0/lib/browser/math.js"> – the global math
<script src="https://cdn.plot.ly/plotly-2.35.2.min.js"> – the global Plotly
mathviz.js, copied into site_libs/quarto-contrib/mathviz-<version>/
mathviz.css, alongside it

The order matters: mathviz.js patches Plotly.newPlot the moment it runs, so Plotly must already be there. Both vendor tags come from CDNs (they’re pinned to the versions the library is tested against); the bundle is served from your own site.

Options
All optional, under a mathviz: key in _quarto.yml or a page’s front matter:
mathviz:
  plotly: false             # your pages draw with D3/canvas/Plot -- skip Plotly
  mathjs: false             # ...or math.js. Either also accepts a URL string
  css: false                # bring your own stylesheet
  referrer: same-origin     # emit <meta name="referrer"> ahead of the CDN tags



Key
Values
Effect




plotly
true (default), false, or a URL
Whether to add the Plotly tag, and from where. With false the Plotly patch is a silent no-op and the VM.plotting theme functions still work for Observable Plot.


mathjs
true (default), false, or a URL
Whether to add the math.js tag, and from where. VM.expressions.* take the instance as an argument, so a page that loads math.js another way passes that.


css
true (default) or false
Whether to add mathviz.css. With false you supply the --vm-* tokens and the ojs-* rules yourself – see Theming.


referrer
a referrer policy string
Emits <meta name="referrer" content="…"> before the CDN tags, so the third-party origins don’t see a page’s path or query string – which on a math page is the reader’s own input. Visual Math Lab uses same-origin.





Versions and updating
quarto update apurvanakade/mathviz            # latest tag
quarto update apurvanakade/mathviz@v0.1.1     # a specific tag
quarto add apurvanakade/mathviz@v0.1.1        # pin at install time
The version names the site_libs/quarto-contrib/mathviz-<version>/ folder in your rendered output, which is what invalidates a browser’s cached copy when you upgrade.


Trying a local checkout
To test a change to the library in your own project before it’s published:
quarto add /path/to/mathviz --no-prompt
A local directory is accepted; Quarto copies _extensions/mathviz/ in. Re-run after each npm run build in the library. A symlink at _extensions/mathviz is not discovered – Quarto checks isDirectory() on the raw directory entry.

title: Markup contract
text:
Panels

ojs-panel
The chrome: padding, a --vm-border border, --vm-radius corners, --vm-surface background. It also restyles every <input>, <select>, <button> and Observable Inputs <form> inside it – consistent height, focus rings in --vm-accent, labels stacked above controls so a row of them bottom-aligns.
It is chrome only. Pair it with ojs-row or ojs-grid for layout. Don’t nest one panel inside another (the border and background double up); nest a bare ojs-row or ojs-grid div instead.


ojs-row
display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-items: flex-end. The first child div gets flex: 1 1 200px and stretches; the last gets flex: 0 0 auto; anything between takes its natural width. That is the shape of most panels: a wide expression field, then a couple of small controls, then a button.

Quarto OJS is the primary host, and several rules target markup mathviz doesn’t own. They are harmless elsewhere, but on a non-Quarto page the corresponding behaviour is simply absent:







Selector

text:
The combinatorics behind a Sperner’s-lemma page: enumerate a uniform triangulation of a triangle in barycentric coordinates, color its vertices, and turn color names into palette colors at the moment of drawing.
Every helper works in the names 'red', 'green', 'blue' – those are the keys the logic compares – and only the three *Color functions at the end touch the actual palette. Keep that split: fill: d => VM.discreteMath.vertexColor(d.color), never fill: "red", which is not the site’s red and doesn’t lighten in dark mode.

title: VM.discreteMath
VM.discreteMath
text:
Triangulation
A uniform order-N triangulation has (N+1)(N+2)/2 vertices, each a triple [i, j, k] of non-negative integers with i + j + k = N; a vertex is a corner when two coordinates are zero and on an edge when one is.

VM.discreteMath.barycentricTriples(N)
Every vertex, i-major.
Returns number[][] – (N+1)(N+2)/2 triples. [[0,0,0]] for N = 0; empty for negative N.

VM.discreteMath.barycentricTriples(2)








VM.discreteMath.subTriangleTriples(N)
The N² small triangles, each as a triple of vertex triples: the N(N+1)/2 “upward” ones first, then the N(N−1)/2 “downward” ones.
Returns number[][][].

VM.discreteMath.subTriangleTriples(2)








VM.discreteMath.triangulationEdges(N)
Every edge exactly once, derived from subTriangleTriples with each interior edge (shared by two triangles) deduplicated.
Returns {a: number[], b: number[]}[].

VM.discreteMath.triangulationEdges(2).length   // 3N(N+1)/2 = 9

title: VM.discreteMath
text:
Coloring

VM.discreteMath.spernerColor(a, b, c)
Colors one vertex so the whole labelling satisfies Sperner’s condition: the corners get fixed colors – (0,0,N) red, (N,0,0) green, (0,N,0) blue – a vertex on a boundary edge gets one of that edge’s two corner colors uniformly at random, and an interior vertex any of the three uniformly at random.
Returns 'red' | 'green' | 'blue'.
Uses Math.random(), so it isn’t reproducible from a seed; a page that needs a URL-shareable coloring draws its own randomness from seededRandom and applies the same three rules.


VM.discreteMath.randomColor()
One of the three names uniformly at random, ignoring position – for showing what breaks when the boundary condition is violated.
Returns 'red' | 'green' | 'blue'.

title: VM.discreteMath
text:
Drawing
These read VM.plotting.colors() / alpha() when called. A cell that stores their output (an array of colored edges, a triangle’s fillColor) must itself depend on chartColors – a bare chartColors; line at the top, as in the live example above – or the stored colors go stale on a toggle.

VM.discreteMath.vertexColor(name)
'red' → colors().alt, 'green' → colors().ok, 'blue' → colors().fn. The prose swatches .vm-swatch-alt / -ok / -accent use the same tokens, so a word and a dot agree.
Returns a CSS color, or null for any other name.


VM.discreteMath.pairColor(colorA, colorB)
The shared color for a pair of distinct names, at 80% opacity: red+green → warn (amber), green+blue → accent3 (teal), red+blue → accent2 (purple). Order doesn’t matter.
Returns an rgba(...) string, or null when the names are equal or the pair isn’t one of the three.


VM.discreteMath.triangleFillColor(colors)
The fill for a small triangle given its vertex names: translucent accent2 (55%) when all three are distinct – a “rainbow” triangle, the object of the lemma – and the string 'none' otherwise.
Returns string.

[VM.discreteMath.vertexColor("red"), VM.discreteMath.pairColor("green", "blue"), VM.discreteMath.triangleFillColor(["red", "green", "blue"]), VM.discreteMath.triangleFillColor(["red", "red", "blue"])]

title: VM.expressions
text:
Every function here takes a math.js instance as its first argument – on a page rendered through the extension that is the global math – and an expression string as typed by a reader. The string is normalized first (trimmed, π replaced by pi), then compiled. Nothing here throws on bad input: an expression that can’t be parsed gives null, and a compiled function that fails at a point (a domain error, say) gives NaN there. Branch on the null and draw an emptyState rather than an empty grid.
The one exception to the pattern is makeRational, which takes no math.js instance and parses only literals.

title: API reference
text: The bundle attaches one global, VM, with a namespace per concern. Each source file adds one function (a few add two or three that belong together) and nothing here has hidden state beyond what’s noted – the theme functions read CSS at call time, the self-installing UI modules keep track of what they’ve enhanced.

title: API reference
text:
Conventions
These hold across the whole surface, so each page states only its exceptions.
Bad input gives null, not an exception. Anything that parses reader-typed text (makeFunction, makeNumber, makeRational) returns null when it can’t; a fit with too few points returns null. Branch on it and draw an emptyState.
Outside a distribution’s support you get 0. Never NaN, so a slider at an invalid parameter flattens a curve rather than breaking the chart.
math.js is passed in, not imported. VM.expressions.* and polynomialFit take the math.js instance as their first argument – the global math on a page rendered through the extension. The one exception is makeRational, which parses literals only and takes no instance.
Colors are read when you ask, not when the page loads. colors(), alpha() and the three discreteMath color helpers return whatever the active theme says right now. Call them inside the cell that builds the traces, and make that cell depend on vmTheme so it re-runs on a toggle – see onThemeChange.
Self-installing modules take no call. The Plotly patch, slider playback, the draggable legend, the SVG fullscreen button and the slider-track fill all find their markup themselves. What each looks for, and how to opt out, is in the markup contract.

title: API reference
text:
Where the signatures live
Every function’s JSDoc in src/js/<category>/<name>.js is the authoritative signature; these pages restate it with context and a live example. A test (src/docs-coverage.test.js) fails the build if a VM.* member exists without a heading here, or vice versa, so the two can’t drift.

Everything a chart needs to look like part of the page: one theme read live from the --vm-* tokens, applied to Plotly and Observable Plot alike, and following the light/dark toggle the moment it flips.

VM.plotting.colors()
A fresh snapshot of the chart palette for whichever theme is active right now, read from the --vm-color-<name> tokens. Keyed by role, not hue, so a page reads colors.fn rather than repeating "#2563eb".









Key

Any argument is ignored. The idiom VM.plotting.colors(vmTheme) exists purely to make the OJS cell depend on vmTheme – see onThemeChange.

chartColors







{
  const row = document.createElement("div")
  row.style.cssText = "display:flex;gap:.5rem;flex-wrap:wrap"
  for (const name of Object.keys(chartColors)) {
    const chip = document.createElement("div")
    chip.style.cssText = `width:5.5rem;padding:.4rem .5rem;border-radius:6px;border:1px solid var(--vm-border);background:${VM.plotting.alpha(chartColors[name], 0.25)};font:12px var(--vm-font-sans)`

  }
  return row
}








VM.plotting.colorway()
The trace color cycle – colors() in role order minus halo, so a trace Plotly or Plot colors automatically never lands on the background color. Already set on layout() and plotOptions().
Returns string[]: [fn, alt, ok, muted, ink, warn, accent2, accent3].


VM.plotting.alpha(token, opacity)
The same hue as a palette token (or any color string) at a given opacity, for a translucent fill that pairs with a solid stroke. An rgba(...) literal stays light-mode-colored after a toggle while its own stroke lightens, so fill and stroke drift apart; this doesn’t.








Parameter
Type
Description




token
string
A palette role ("fn", "ok", …) resolved through colors(), or a #rgb / #rrggbb / rgb(...) / rgba(...) string.


opacity
number
0..1; not clamped.



Returns "rgba(r, g, b, opacity)". An input that can’t be parsed (a CSS named color, hsl(...), a non-string) is returned unchanged.

[VM.plotting.alpha("ok", 0.2), VM.plotting.alpha("#ff0000", 0.5), VM.plotting.alpha("rebeccapurple", 0.5)]

Replaces each digit with its Unicode subscript, for iteration labels in Plotly trace text – which is plain text with no markup, so "x_0" renders with a literal underscore.

title: VM.plotting
text:
Theme detection

VM.plotting.themeName()
Which theme is active right now, by testing the dark selector against <body> and then <html>.
Returns "light" | "dark" ("light" when there is no document).

vmTheme   // this cell re-runs on every toggle -- try it








VM.plotting.onThemeChange(callback)
Calls callback(themeName()) now, synchronously, and again after every real theme change. It observes class and data-bs-theme on both <body> and <html>, waits two animation frames (Quarto flips the class and swaps the stylesheet as separate steps, class first), and compares the theme name before calling – so unrelated body-class churn (a sidebar opening) fires nothing.



Parameter
Type
Description




callback
(theme: "light" \| "dark") => void




Returns () => void, a teardown that disconnects the observer (a no-op when there’s no document.body or MutationObserver; the initial call still happens).
The shape is exactly what Generators.observe wants, which gives the two-line pattern every chart page needs:
vmTheme = Generators.observe(notify => VM.plotting.onThemeChange(notify))
chartColors = VM.plotting.colors(vmTheme)
Now any cell that reads chartColors re-runs on a toggle. This is what makes trace colors follow the theme. Chart chrome (axes, grid, tooltip) is re-themed for you by a relayout the patch performs, but a color you baked into a trace is a value the page chose, and only re-running the cell changes it.


VM.plotting.configure(overrides?)
Adjusts the module’s settings. The only setting is darkSelector: the selector list that means “dark mode”, tested against <body> and <html>. Default:
body.quarto-dark, html[data-bs-theme="dark"], body[data-bs-theme="dark"], html.vm-dark, body.vm-dark
A site whose toggle uses none of these calls VM.plotting.configure({darkSelector: ".my-dark"}) once at load, and declares its dark --vm-* tokens under that same selector. Keep the selectors root-scoped (html/body); an unscoped [data-bs-theme="dark"] matches Quarto’s <nav> and leaks the dark palette into the navbar.








Parameter
Type
Description




overrides
{darkSelector?: string}
Merged in when it’s an object; anything else is ignored. Keys are not validated.



Returns a copy of the settings now in effect.

title: VM.plotting
text:
Building a chart

VM.plotting.layout(overrides?)
The shared Plotly layout, themed from the live tokens:

transparent paper_bgcolor / plot_bgcolor, so the page’s own background shows through (no #E5ECF6 plate, no white box in dark mode)
font in --vm-font-sans, --vm-text; axes, ticks, gridlines in --vm-text-soft / --vm-border / --vm-grid, automargin: true
colorway(), hoverLabel(), themed modebar colors, textfont for trace labels
a transition of 300 ms cubic-in-out (0 under prefers-reduced-motion; while a slider playback sweep runs, shortened to the gap between values so the tween lands before the next one arrives)
small non-zero margin ({l: 8, r: 12, t: 12, b: 8}) that automargin grows as needed









Parameter
Type
Description




overrides
object (optional)
Deep-merged on top, so {xaxis: {title: "x", range: [0, 1]}} extends the shared axis chrome rather than replacing it. Arrays and primitives replace wholesale.



Returns a Plotly layout object.






Don’t pass margin: {l: 0, r: 0, t: 0, b: 0}



It was a common convention and it defeats automargin: the rotated y-title and tick labels end up jammed against the container edge.


With the patch installed this is merged under every newPlot/react layout automatically. Calling it explicitly is harmless and makes the dependency visible.


VM.plotting.config(overrides?)
{responsive: true, displaylogo: false}, deep-merged with overrides. The patch also applies this and then sets the modebar button list on top.


VM.plotting.hoverLabel()
The themed tooltip style: --vm-surface background, --vm-border border, left-aligned, 12 px --vm-font-sans in --vm-text.
It has to be set on each trace, not only the layout – Plotly derives a trace’s tooltip background from that trace’s own color unless the trace sets hoverlabel itself, so a layout-level default never actually shows. The patch injects it onto every trace that doesn’t set one. Call it yourself only for a chart built outside the patch.


VM.plotting.emptyState(message)
A centered message for an empty plot area, as an annotations array. Use it whenever the page’s computation bailed out; without it an unparseable input draws an empty grid indistinguishable from a valid-but-empty result.
annotations: f ? [] : VM.plotting.emptyState("Couldn't parse that expression")
Returns a one-element Plotly annotations array at paper coordinates (0.5, 0.5) in --vm-text-soft.


VM.plotting.autoResize(div)
Keeps a graph div sized to its container, and stops once the div leaves the document. Every chart built detached (the usual OJS pattern: create a div, Plotly.newPlot into it, return it) needs this, because Plotly measures 0×0 at newPlot time. A bare ResizeObserver outlives its div and throws "Resize must be passed a displayed plot div element." once a re-run replaces it; this one disconnects itself.
Returns the ResizeObserver, or null where ResizeObserver doesn’t exist. Skips resizing while the div is hidden (display: none) and is safe when Plotly isn’t loaded.

number[]

Buttons




1
download PNG


2
box zoom, pan


3
zoom in, zoom out (each step scales the visible span by 1.25×, not Plotly’s 2×, which overshoots when framing a curve), autoscale, reset


4
fullscreen



Box select and lasso are absent. The list is spelled out as config.modeBarButtons, replacing whatever a page passes there – which is safe only because every chart the library targets is 2-D cartesian.
a relayout(themePatch()) on every theme flip

The patch is idempotent and a silent no-op when Plotly isn’t on the page (mathviz: {plotly: false}).

VM.plotting.installPlotlyPatch()
Runs the patch. Only needed when Plotly arrives later than the bundle and DOMContentLoaded – a dynamic import, say.
Returns true once patched (also when already patched); false when Plotly isn’t on the page.


VM.plotting.fullscreenButton
The fullscreen modebar button, as a Plotly custom-button object: {name: "fullscreen", title, icon: {width, height, path}, click(gd)}. The patch adds it to every chart; a page touches this only to reuse its glyph (VM.plotting.fullscreenButton.icon – Bootstrap Icons’ arrows-fullscreen), or to add it to a chart built outside the patch via modeBarButtonsToAdd.
Clicking fullscreens the nearest .ojs-chart-block – so the controls bar and legend come along – or, without one, the graph div itself; a second click exits. Before entering it records the chart’s aspect ratio as --vm-plot-aspect-ratio on the div so the CSS can letterbox it.

text:
SVG fullscreen helpers
Charts drawn as inline SVG (Observable Plot, hand-built <svg>) have no modebar. Give the wrapper class="ojs-chart-block ojs-svg-block" and the library appends one persistent fullscreen button pinned to the figure’s top-right corner – see the markup contract. These two pure helpers are what it measures with; they’re exported for unit tests and for a page that wants to do the same arithmetic.

VM.plotting.svgAspectRatio({…})
Takes {viewBox, width, height}. The width/height ratio an <svg> draws at, from its attributes: a four-part viewBox when it has one, else width/height when both are positive.
Returns number | null (null means “measure it”).

[VM.plotting.svgAspectRatio({viewBox: "0 0 640 400"}), VM.plotting.svgAspectRatio({width: "300", height: "150"}), VM.plotting.svgAspectRatio({})]

The smallest box containing every given {left, top, right, bottom}.
Returns {left, top, right, bottom} | null (null for an empty list).

title: VM.ui
text:
Most of what VM.ui does needs no call at all. Three modules are self-installing: they watch the page for the markup they enhance and attach themselves to it whenever it appears, including elements Observable Inputs recreates on a re-run.
The callable API is four functions: a legend that is also an Observable view, a table renderer, an “apply this example” helper, and the pure arithmetic behind playback (exported for tests and for anyone building their own).
VM = window.VM
vmTheme = Generators.observe(notify => VM.plotting.onThemeChange(notify))
chartColors = VM.plotting.colors(vmTheme)

title: VM.ui
text:
Legend

VM.ui.legendOverlay(items, options?)
A floating legend of clickable swatch+label rows that toggles which traces a chart shows, replacing Plotly’s built-in legend. It implements Observable Inputs’ view contract (a value property, an "input" event on change), so it slots into viewof exactly like an Inputs.checkbox:
viewof shown = VM.ui.legendOverlay([{label: "f(x)", color: chartColors.fn}, {label: "f'(x)", color: chartColors.alt}])
and shown is the array of checked labels. Put the cell inside the chart’s .ojs-chart-block: the CSS floats it over the chart’s top-left corner, and the draggable-legend module picks it up.









Parameter
Type
Default
Description




items
{label, color}[]

Rows, in display order.


options.value
string[]
every label
The initially checked labels.



Returns an HTMLDivElement (div.ojs-legend-overlay) with:

a value accessor – getter returns the checked labels in items order (string[]); the setter accepts any iterable (null clears all) and re-renders
a bubbling "input" event on each user toggle (click, Enter, Space) – not on a programmatic value set, matching Observable Inputs and the set-then-dispatch protocol applyExampleParams uses

It uses only DOM APIs – no htl or Inputs dependency – so it works on a plain page too.


viewof legendShown = VM.ui.legendOverlay([
  {label: "sin", color: chartColors.fn},
  {label: "cos", color: chartColors.alt},
  {label: "sin·cos", color: chartColors.ok}
])







{
  const xs = [], s = [], c = [], sc = []
  for (let i = 0; i <= 200; i++) { const x = -Math.PI + 2 * Math.PI * i / 200; xs.push(x); s.push(Math.sin(x)); c.push(Math.cos(x)); sc.push(Math.sin(x) * Math.cos(x)) }
  const data = [
    {name: "sin", x: xs, y: s, line: {color: chartColors.fn}},
    {name: "cos", x: xs, y: c, line: {color: chartColors.alt}},
    {name: "sin·cos", x: xs, y: sc, line: {color: chartColors.ok}}
  ]
  for (const trace of data) trace.visible = legendShown.includes(trace.name) ? true : "legendonly"
  const div = document.createElement("div")
  div.style.height = "300px"
  Plotly.newPlot(div, data, {showlegend: false, xaxis: {title: "x"}})
  VM.plotting.autoResize(div)
  return div
}








legendShown






Try dragging the legend by its grip (appears on hover), then reload – the position is remembered.


Draggable legend
The grip on the legend above is added by a self-installing module. It clamps the panel to the chart block, re-clamps on resize and fullscreen, supports the keyboard (arrows move 10 px, Shift+arrow 1 px, Home resets) and double-click to reset, and persists the offset in localStorage. It deliberately does not touch .ojs-chart-controls, which sits in normal flow above the chart and has nothing to be dragged clear of. The two pure helpers behind it:


VM.ui.clampOverlayOffset({…})
Clamps a proposed drag offset so no part of the panel leaves its container. Takes one object: {dx, dy, offsetLeft, offsetTop, width, height, containerWidth, containerHeight}. dx/dy are the proposed offset; offsetLeft/offsetTop the panel’s layout position (transforms don’t affect layout, so they stay a fixed reference); width/height the panel’s size; containerWidth/containerHeight the block’s.
Returns {dx, dy}. A panel larger than its container is pinned to the near edge rather than given a crossed range.


VM.ui.overlayStorageKey(pathname, role, index)
The localStorage key a dragged panel’s offset is kept under: `vml-overlay-pos:${pathname}:${role}:${index}`. The module uses location.pathname, "legend", and the panel’s .ojs-chart-block index on the page; the stored value is JSON.stringify({dx, dy}).

VM.ui.overlayStorageKey("/apps/newton-method/", "legend", 0)

{

title: VM.ui
text:
Example presets

VM.ui.applyExampleParams(fieldSelectors, params, triggerEl)
Applies an example’s parameter values to the page’s viewof fields, then clicks the page’s own “plot”/“run” button so the normal commit flow runs – no reload, no scroll jump. This is what a “Try an example” dropdown calls.








Parameter
Type
Description




fieldSelectors
{paramKey: cssSelector}
Plain strings, looked up fresh with document.querySelector each time – e.g. {fx: '[data-example-field="fx"]'}. Tag each targetable field with a stable data-example-field attribute in the cell that owns it.


params
{paramKey: value}
Applied in insertion order with a 100 ms wait after each (including the last), so a field whose bounds depend on an earlier one sees its freshly recreated view. Order upstream fields first. Keys with no selector, or whose element isn’t on the page, are skipped.


triggerEl
Element
An element containing the <button> to click at the end. Must not be null (throws); the click is skipped if it holds no button.



Returns Promise<void>.
Two rules that come from how Observable’s runtime behaves, both learned the hard way:






Pass selectors, not viewof references



A cell that references a view whose identity is reactively recreated – a step slider capped by a “max” field – becomes reactive on it. Since this function is what changes that upstream field, a version taking direct references re-triggers itself in a loop with no natural end. A querySelector at the moment of use carries no reactive dependency.








Call it from a plain DOM listener, never from a cell reactive on a <select>



A native <select> fires both input and change per selection, so a reactive cell runs twice, and two overlapping calls race – observed corrupting a field’s final value when the second cascade landed after the first. Attach one listener to a stable element instead. The try-an-example recipe shows the full wiring.

title: VM.ui
text:
Slider playback
Every range slider inside an .ojs-panel or .ojs-chart-controls gets a play/pause button and a small caret that opens a popover of speed presets (¼× – 4×) and a mode (Once / Loop / Bounce). Playback is requestAnimationFrame-driven, so the motion is smooth rather than a stepped jump; it stops when the reader grabs the slider, when the tab is hidden, when a re-run detaches the slider, and at the end of a Once sweep (the button becomes a replay glyph). At most one sweep runs per page.



viewof playDemo = Inputs.range([0, 2 * Math.PI], {label: "phase (press ▶)", step: 0.05, value: 0})








{
  const xs = [], ys = []
  for (let i = 0; i <= 300; i++) { const x = 4 * Math.PI * i / 300; xs.push(x); ys.push(Math.sin(x - playDemo)) }
  const div = document.createElement("div")
  div.style.height = "220px"
  Plotly.newPlot(div, [{x: xs, y: ys, line: {color: chartColors.fn, width: 2.5}}], {showlegend: false, yaxis: {range: [-1.2, 1.2]}, margin: {t: 8}})
  VM.plotting.autoResize(div)
  return div
}







The chosen speed and mode are a viewing preference, shared by every slider on the site and stored in localStorage["vm-playback"] as {speed, mode} – deliberately not URL-synced like the page’s inputs, since they’re not part of the computation a shared link reproduces.
The sweep’s length scales with the slider’s own stop count – about 350 ms per stop, clamped to 2–10 s – which is what lets the module enhance every slider with no per-page tuning. A page opts a slider out with data-vm-play="off" on the input or an ancestor:


{
  const wrap = document.createElement("div")
  wrap.dataset.vmPlay = "off"
  wrap.appendChild(Inputs.range([0, 10], {label: "data-vm-play=\"off\": no play button", step: 1, value: 3}))
  return wrap
}







Inputs.range([0, 10], {label: "a sibling without it", step: 1, value: 3})













Why the popover is a native [popover]



It renders in the browser’s top layer. Quarto wraps every OJS output in .cell-output-display with overflow: auto, which clips any descendant that escapes its box – a panel opening above a 37 px cell was cut to a sliver. No z-index fixes a clip; only leaving it does, and the top layer is outside every ancestor’s clip. This applies to any floating UI inside any OJS cell: reach for [popover], not a nested absolute box.



VM.ui.playbackDuration({…})
Takes one object: {min, max, step, speed}. Total length of one end-to-end sweep, in ms: 350 ms × stops, clamped to [2000, 10000], divided by speed. A non-finite or non-positive step (a slider with step="any") counts as 100 stops; a non-finite or non-positive speed as 1.
Returns number; 0 when the slider can’t be swept (max ≤ min, or a non-finite bound).

[VM.ui.playbackDuration({min: 0, max: 10, step: 1, speed: 1}), VM.ui.playbackDuration({min: 0, max: 100, step: 1, speed: 2}), VM.ui.playbackDuration({min: 0, max: 0, step: 1, speed: 1})]








VM.ui.playbackFrame({…})
Takes one object: {min, max, step, elapsed, duration, mode, start}. Where the thumb should be after elapsed ms of a sweep of length duration that began at fraction start of the track. mode is "once", "loop" (sawtooth) or "bounce" (triangle wave); anything else behaves as "once".
Returns {value, direction, done} – value snapped to the step grid (by whole-step count from min, then trimmed to 12 significant digits, then clamped into [min, max]); direction is −1 only on a bounce’s return leg; done is true once a "once" sweep reaches the end, and for any degenerate input.

VM.ui.playbackFrame({min: 0, max: 10, step: 0.5, elapsed: 750, duration: 3000, mode: "bounce", start: 0})








VM.ui.playbackTweenMs
A number, not a function: the chart transition length VM.plotting.layout() should use right now. 0 while no sweep is running; during one, 90% of the gap between consecutive slider values, capped at 300 ms, so each tween settles just before the next value arrives instead of a flat 300 ms overrunning a faster gap and leaving the chart permanently mid-tween. Read it if you build your own layout; don’t set it.

VM.ui.playbackTweenMs

title: Troubleshooting
text: Each of these has happened on a real page. The cause is usually one of three things: a token read from the wrong element, a value baked in at build time that should have been read at draw time, or a wrapper class missing from the markup.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Charts and theme
The chart has a pale blue plot area, or a white box, on the dark theme. The layout isn’t themed. On a page rendered through the extension the Plotly patch merges layout() under every chart, so this means either Plotly loaded after mathviz.js (a hand-written <script> order; the extension gets it right) or the page passed mathviz: {plotly: false} and loads Plotly itself. Fix the order, or call VM.plotting.installPlotlyPatch() after Plotly is available.
The axes and grid follow the toggle but the traces stay light-mode colored. Trace colors are values the page baked in; only re-running the cell changes them. Add the two-line pattern at the top of the page and read chartColors.fn in the chart cell – Theming: following the theme.
A translucent fill stays light-mode colored while its stroke lightens. An rgba(...) literal. Use VM.plotting.alpha("ok", 0.2) and make the cell depend on chartColors.
The hover tooltip is a white box with unreadable text on the dark theme. Two possible causes. If it’s your own token-reading code: you read from document.documentElement; the dark tokens are declared on selectors matching <body>, so <html> reports light values – read from document.body (why). If it’s a chart built outside the patch: Plotly derives a trace’s tooltip background from the trace’s own color unless the trace sets hoverlabel; set hoverLabel() on each trace, not only on the layout.
A marker’s white ring is invisible in dark mode / glaring in light mode. line: {color: "white"}. Use chartColors.halo – white on light, the page background on dark.
Colors read in a cell are correct after a toggle, but a stored array of colored things isn’t. The storing cell ran before the toggle and doesn’t depend on the theme. Add a bare chartColors; line at the top of it.
The theme toggles but my onThemeChange callback sees the old colors. You aren’t using onThemeChange. Quarto flips the body class and swaps the stylesheet as separate steps; a synchronous observer reads the outgoing theme. onThemeChange waits two frames for this reason.
The whole chart rebuilds when the sidebar opens, or on some unrelated interaction. A body-class observer with no theme comparison. onThemeChange compares themeName() inside its deferred callback and fires only on a real change; use it rather than a bare MutationObserver.
The dark palette leaks into the navbar on a light page. A dark selector that isn’t root-scoped – a bare [data-bs-theme="dark"]. Quarto sets that attribute on its <nav>. Match on html/body only, in both tokens.css and configure({darkSelector}).
Resize must be passed a displayed plot div element. A ResizeObserver outliving its div: the cell re-ran, built a new div, and the old observer kept firing on the detached one. Use autoResize, which disconnects itself.
The y-axis title and tick labels are jammed against the container edge. margin: {l: 0, r: 0, t: 0, b: 0} in the page’s layout, which defeats automargin. Remove it; layout() provides small non-zero margins that automargin grows.
An unparseable formula draws an empty grid. Branch on the null from makeFunction and pass emptyState as the annotations.
The chart is 0 px tall / doesn’t appear. The graph div has no height. Give it plotly-box-large or a style.height, and call autoResize – the div was built detached, so Plotly measured 0×0.
Zoom in/out jumps too far; there’s a box-select button I don’t want. The patch isn’t installed (see the first item). It replaces the modebar with 1.25× zoom steps and no select tools.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Panels and controls
The legend disappeared / appears as a thin strip. The legend cell isn’t inside an .ojs-chart-block. Quarto’s .cell-output-display is a scroll container that clips escaping descendants; the block’s rules turn that off for the cells inside it.
A floating panel I built is cut in half. Same clip. No z-index fixes it; only leaving the clip does. Render floating UI as a native [popover] (top layer), as the playback popover does.
Two-column grid overflows the right edge by ~70 px. Observable Inputs’ forms have a fixed 360px width. The ojs-panel rules override it – the controls aren’t inside a panel.
Labels wrap onto three lines above a slider. Observable’s 120px label column. Inside .ojs-panel or .ojs-chart-controls labels are freed; outside them they aren’t.
Doubled border and background around a panel. An ojs-panel nested inside another. Nest a bare ojs-row/ojs-grid div instead.
A slider has no play button. It isn’t inside .ojs-panel or .ojs-chart-controls, or something above it has data-vm-play="off", or it has no <form> ancestor (a raw <input type="range"> outside Observable Inputs).
The playback popover opens under the navbar / off the right edge. Shouldn’t happen – it clears #quarto-header, .navbar.fixed-top and the window edge. If your site’s fixed header uses another selector, the panel may open under it; file an issue with the selector.
applyExampleParams applies the first fields and then a later one snaps back. Field order: a field whose bounds depend on an earlier one (a step slider capped by “max”) must come after it in params. Or: you called it from a cell reactive on a <select>, which fires twice per selection; call it from one DOM listener on a stable element.
applyExampleParams loops forever / the page freezes with history-API throttling. fieldSelectors holds viewof references instead of selector strings. See why.
A table renders unstyled. renderTable emits Bootstrap classes (table table-sm table-bordered). On a non-Bootstrap page bring your own table styles or target .ojs-table-container table.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Build and install
quarto add says the extension isn’t found, or a symlinked _extensions/mathviz isn’t used. Quarto checks isDirectory() on the raw directory entry, so a symlink is skipped. Use quarto add /path/to/mathviz --no-prompt, which copies.
Version mismatch: package.json=… _extension.yml=… mathviz.lua=… The build refuses to run until the three agree. Bump all three.
CI fails with “dist/ is out of date”. A change under src/ without npm run build. Run it and commit dist/ and _extensions/mathviz/dist/.
(intermediate value)(...) is not a function on page load. Two source files concatenated without a ; between them (})(window) followed by (function parses as a call). The build inserts the separator; this only appears if dist/ was hand-edited or built another way.
A new function isn’t in window.VM in the browser. Its file isn’t listed in src/manifest.mjs – npm test fails with the name. Add it after anything it reads at load time.
npm test fails with “documents … but exported …”. The docs-coverage test: a VM.* member exists without a ### VM.<category>.<name> heading in docs/reference/<category>.qmd, or a heading names something that doesn’t exist. Add or fix the entry.
